This might be the best game Adam has ever made. Of course after WTTG2.As a huge WWTG2 fan, let's admit that WTTG2 and Scrutinized made you feel incredibly in the loop while you're playing them. After discovering the game, it felt like you were just trying to beat it as a challenge to yourself.

But things changed in Dead Signal. The dialogues in the game, as well as the clearly presented story, make you feel like you are playing a completely real-time story game. It kind of stops being a challenge and leaves you exploring the story and wondering what the next move is.

As someone who loves the horror genre, Reflect Studios' productions have always impressed me. Especially Adam's meticulousness in his work, storytelling and the change of game mechanics fascinate me.

A truly successful game. Definitely worth the money

The game is good and fun. It essentially is I'm On Observation Duty with extra steps and more gameplay. It's similar to Adams' other games and keeps that paranoia-type spookiness he's great at making for his games. The skill ceiling is also way lower than Welcome To The Game II, in fact, it's probably the easiest game Adam has made so far, so it's pretty accessible for those who don't want to have to learn a bunch of mechanics or get overwhelmed from the sheer amount of things to do, which I can appreciate. 

There's really only one big issue that I have that honestly really drags the game down for me, and that's the extreme performance issues. I can run Adams' other games on the highest settings no issue, however with this game, any setting on High and up causes extreme lag and frame rate problems for me that just should not be happening, especially if I can run Welcome To The Game II just fine, which is probably Adams' biggest game at the time of this review, correct me if I'm wrong. I don't know if this was just a case of poor optimization or somehow the game is just that demanding of specs but it is a big issue especially when lower settings mess with textures of things, making it sometimes really hard to tell what you're looking at.

I would definitely recommend this game, but do be warned that you'll likely have to play it on lower graphic settings. Hopefully it gets patched/fixed though.

I'm really glad Adam had a return to form making this game. Gives a lot of the vibes WTTG2 did in a good way, while cutting down on some of the more cryptic and frustrating elements. It's definitely not as hard. 

I have two critiques. The first concerns the decision to make the Noir talk, specifically the lady. Part of what made them so creepy was their total silence. It takes away a lot of the creepiness to hear them. I understand it's to avoid some frustration with her mechanic of getting close, but you should have more faith in your players to do it, or maybe instead of her speaking she could gesture for you to come closer. 

Secondly, I feel as though there needs to be a short grace period after dealing with threats, at least in the non-nightmare modes. Multiple times now I've had to deal with female Noir on the roof, only to get shot by Lucas two seconds later without even realizing the laser was there. 

Good job on the game besides that.

Really good. Glad to see the dev really branch out this time and probably reach a larger audience with options for casual and hardcore players alike. I think I own all of the games this guy has made unless there was something before WTTG. But this is the first one I'm actually playing for more than five minutes before deciding I'd rather not poop my pants and just go watch a YouTuber play instead. You are still very much in danger, but (without spoiling the mechanics I believe I have down so far) each death seems fair and explainable, which in turn makes you feel like you are learning how to combat your enemies instead of just getting frustrated. (Except for the one time I got sniped in the bedroom even though there was absolutely no angle to make such a shot, I think I know why, but I'm still going to keep this mechanic spoiler free). The main goal of the game, which others have already pointed out is like Observation Duty, is also much more interesting and fun to me then looking for hidden keys on websites in my opinion. Overall I think it's great, I'm glad to see this dev is still making games, I thought the final game from Reflect was going to be Rides with Strangers, so either I was mistaken, or he has decided to continue on developing. I sincerely hope that future games after this also continue the same trend of appealing to all horror players instead of the hardest of the hardcore. Scrutinized showed a step in that direction, and Dead Signal has brought it where it needed to be in order to be accessible to all. Great work Adam, people love your style, myself included, and the world that you have built with everything interconnecting. I think the key, which you must already be well aware of, is that this world feels grounded in reality. There's no ghosts, or wizards, or impossible experiments gone wrong. Each game feels like it could potentially happen to a person who was just in the worst place at the worst time, while being involved with the wrong things. The only thing all these characters lack is the common sense to call the police, but hey, if that was the case there would be no game.

[h1] Dead Signal is nerve-wrecking. [/h1]

The constant threat of killers who [b]will[/b] get you if you’re not paying attention kept me on edge like no other horror game. Most horror games make a big deal out of their monster showing up—[b]not Dead Signal.[/b] Here, you have to notice the laser sight in your window without the game spelling it out for you. You have to realize there’s a man in your bathroom, [i]even though you locked the door.[/i] Speaking of which… get used to the code randomly changing and unlocking the door. If you miss that, well, good luck.

[hr][/hr]
[h2] What I Liked: [/h2]

✔ [b]The Gameplay Loop[/b] – I love how it mixes checking cameras, delivering packages, and hiding from killers. It keeps things from getting stale and makes every run feel intense.
✔ [b]The Killers[/b] – They’re all unique, and honestly, I even liked dying to some of them. Unfortunately, I got spoiled on a few mechanics beforehand, but the deaths still caught me off guard. Most of the time, I feel like I only die because I messed up—except when it comes to Lucas. More on that later.
✔ [b]The Atmosphere[/b] – This game is [i]constantly[/i] making me paranoid. If I spend more than 20 seconds watching the cameras, I feel like I [i]have to[/i] check the apartment. The male Noir, especially, makes sure I never get too comfortable.
✔ [b]More Accessible Than WTTG2[/b] – It has a lot in common with Welcome to the Game 2 (the whole "killers trying to stop you while you use a computer" thing), but unlike WTTG2, Dead Signal doesn’t make you deal with disturbing websites. It keeps the horror focused on the [i]gameplay[/i], which I appreciate.

[hr][/hr]
[h2] What I Didn’t Like: [/h2]

✖ [b]Lucas Can Just Kill You With No Warning[/b] – If he spawns while you're in or entering the hallway, he can kill you [i]instantly[/i] when you take the elevator to the roof. I lost a run in the last hour of the night to this and couldn’t figure out what I did wrong, even after rewatching my recording. Apparently, I’m not the only one this has happened to. If it’s a bug, I hope it gets patched. If not, at least give us some way to tell he’s there.
✖ [b]Camera Jumpscares[/b] – It’s not the actual scare that gets me, it’s the [i]loud, obnoxious[/i] sound effect. Thankfully, they don’t happen often, but still.
✖ [b]The 1% Elevator Death Chance[/b] – I [i]hate[/i] this. The elevator is [i]way[/i] faster with the breaker flipped, so I can’t go back to using it the slow way. But losing a run to pure RNG? That just feels bad.

Dead Signal may be the best game by Adam yet.
I loved WttG 2 I had a blast trying to make up strategies and plans to reach the end of the night. I didn't like Scrutinized, as the threats seemed too RNG and the task you were given was... kinda boring imo.
But Dead Signal reminded me why I loved WttG and fell in love with this kind of games. I only played version 2.0, mind you, that apparently came with a lot more strategy, upgrades and stuff to do in the game, so I have *no* idea how the game was before.
This game has a lot of RNG, a lot more than WttG 2, there's so much stuff going on you need to pay attention to that sometimes it can be frustrating and even make you fail a perfectly good run.
And yet, I still think that this is the best game Adam has ever made. This game has well designed mechanics that work very well together. Problems and tasks that force you out of your room where threats can lurk and try to kill you, tools that give you a very nice advantage while wasting reports that could make you reach your quota, threats that force you away from your PC while you need to get those reports in to reach said quota. Everything works very well together.
There's a lot of things you will have to manage and defend yourself from here, but the most threatening is your own stress.

The only complain I have, as I said, is that there's a little too much RNG sometimes, and getting a game over after hours of a perfectly good run is very frustrating.

The gameplay loop is extremely enjoyable and the game feels pretty polished. I like the storyline and other elements related to the worldbuilding, like the contunity of some of the antagonists like Lucas. The game while tight feels very fair once you have a full grasp of the mechanics, although said mechanics can be relatively difficult for newplayers trying to learn by themselves without a guide.

The spotting of strange effects on the camera is also balanced very interestingly. Items are present for a set period of time before disappearing so cameras aren't overloaded with events if you fail to report a lot for a while and it brings up the element of strategy when it comes to leaving the computer to attend other stuff like delivering packages, as you may be missing out on crucial reports you desperately need for the quota. The addition of the hacking program and Lady Lotus who you can choose to act or report to instead for better payment at the trade off of losing a report for your quota is really interesting and once again rewards strategy and gameplan.
My biggest grip with the camera section is the absolute chaos that is Male Noir's spawn. The idea of getting up every now and then to check your appartement is a cool concept, but with Male Noir having the ability to spawn as soon as you sit on the chair could make for some very unfortunate timing since you only have about 20 seconds to get up again if that happens. While the game is totally beatable despite this, it is something I image new players would have trouble realizing and meet some awkward deaths.

Everything going on outside the appartement is great too. The balancing of threats feel done right and is very satisfying to perform correctly. The only event I haven't encountered outside of the appartement is having Mr. Delfalco come to the roof as you're there and having to hide from him so I can't attest to how well it works and how fair it is, however everything else is spot on and will reward players who are paying attention to the environment and the rules.
The only drawback I have with the outside appartement section is the elevator's switch. It's definitely a low risk high reward thing that probably doesn't bother people much, but I can't help but feel bothered by the complete random chance element of it, even if it is allegedly just 1% of a death chance. Having an element that's entirely up to chance in a game where everything can be survived as long as your strategy and awareness is on point feels kind of out of place, and sure, while enabling the lever is your decision, sometime it doesn't feel like it when The Shade sends you to the lower floors of the building multiple times in a row while you're pressed for time on the quotas. And it makes it difficult to care much about the signal booster as well since traveling floors in search of a green zone is very time consuming.
I would fix it by changing the penalty of having the switch on: raise the chance to something above 1%, however should that chance be met, instead of being met with death and the end of your run, the elevator could simply fail and get stuck, either having to wait for it to come back on or performing some kind of minigame on the floor you got stuck on, causing time loss and potential encounters with the Noirs and Delfalco. Food for thoughts though. This whole elevator switch thing is a minor nitpick though I did meet the death twice in 10 hours of gameplay.

Finally, on the horror factor. The game shines the most in the atmosphere departement. This game is constantly accompanied by a wind-y, droning eerie atmosphere sound effect that sets the tone as you're constantly looking either for small reports on your cameras or more dangerously for threats around you, with it only seemingly ceassing on the roof top. With all the threats being mostly silent too, it adds a level of tension and uncertainty. When you're deep in your cameras and you check over your shoulder to see a laser piercing through your window has your mind race as you remember the preferable course of event you should take to avoid it while wondering how long it's been there and if you'll even have the time to go and hide. And the upgrades are a perfect counterbalance to this. I've only really played with the Thermometer upgrade (and a couple of cams fixer and scans here and there), and having the sudden loud buzzing of the thermometer announcing a threat in your appartement while you're deep scrutinizing your screen is pretty starteling.
To the countrary to the masterful ambiance of the game, the more "straightforward" horror elements such as the camera jumpscares kind of fail for me. The models just appearing all of a sudden on a camera and poofing out of existence feels too unrealistic to be really scary and the bald head of the motel room feels pretty cheap and ineffective after the first time you get it. And pretty ugly looking too on anything but the epic graphics quality (which I didn't get to play on as either the game struggles with optimization or my relatively beef PC isn't so beef for Dead Signal in particular).

Additionally, while it does set a character trait, Delfalco's whistling as he arrives to your appartement also feels a bit too forced in universe to be believable at least to me. I can buy the Noirs being some kind of crazy efficient killing ninja who just so happen to not kill you right away because they abide by Adam's set of rules, but Delfalco, as far as I'm aware, as no relation to Adam or the want to "play games" with his victim/witnesses, and that whisteling really has it feel like he's trying to warn Ronald that he's coming on purpose. I would find it much scarier if instead of it being the indicator that he's arriving, you instead heard the distant ding of the elevator and the approaching footsteps. Sure from the computer, the footsteps wouldn't be as audible, but it would reward players paying enough attention to hear the ding and serve as a much more stressful moment for those who missed it and only get to hear the loud steps of Delfalco who is already much too close to the door by now for you to make it to safety, let alone turn off any light.

I want a small note on the graphics too. The game overall looks good even if the models are of okay quality (at least on the graphics setting I'm playing on). I understand and am completely fine not experiencing the best of quality when I'm not playing on the best of graphics. However as I played on a mix of Mid to High settings with my own custom settings, I've run into issues such as textures glitching and twitching as you walk around them (and on the cameras as well which kind of distracts and makes it harder to find the stuff you're looking for), item icons bugging, and have the elevator numbers disappear, having to then take a second or two to calculate the floor I wanted to go to because of it. I'm not sure what causes this but I would really like a fix for this on the general Mid quality settings, even if the cost turns out to be a greater loss of polish on the game's looks, since it does tamper with gameplay in a pretty annoying way.


Overall, a very solid horror and tense experience that you can enjoy for quite the handful of hours (and a lot more if you want to get all of the achievements or try your luck with Nightmare mode, which I'm still personally building up the will power to even launch). It's fairly stressful and tense, usually delivers well on the horror factor, it's replayable, and the story works well with it and how the game tries to rationalize in universe everything that's going on.

10 hours to the count and I really do recommend this title for those with the dedication and heart prowess to invest in this great title!

As far as indie horror games go, it's very solid. Reflect Studios games tend to excel at creating very on-edge and tense gameplay because of the balance between necessary task-focus while threats are hunting you at the same time, and that design is well executed here. 

Gameplay-wise, it's like a mix of 
- Observation Duty (spotting things on cameras and filing reports)
- Scrutinized (meeting quotas, buying upgrades, watching cameras)
- Welcome to the Game II (some of the threats and killers from that game are back)

Your attention has to be fully on one thing at a time by design, and you're punished for not staying on top of things. The difficulty also really contributes to the feeling of tension. There is some RNG and unpredictability which does affect the gameplay, but it's not nearly as complicated or deep as Welcome to the Game II was in terms of gameplay. While Welcome to the Game II had very in-depth hacking and minigames, Dead Signal has greatly simplified that, which may be a good thing if you're not looking for something so mechanically-complex.

There are bugs which can be annoying, but they don't happen too often.
I think it's a fair price for the value you get. If you enjoyed previous Reflect Studios games, you'll most likely enjoy this one.

Version 2.0 of this nervous breakdown simulator is out and since it's now a completely different game, I have to revise the review. The game is still Welcome to the Game-lite with Observation Duty elements added to it, but it is now more Welcome to the Game which fixes a few flaws with the 1.x version of the game. Version 2.0 adds currency, upgrades, a nightmare difficulty with a new killer and strategic choices in the form of multiple entities to report things to which pays out more but at the cost of increasing the time pressure that he game puts on you which given it's very random nature can be a nail biter. This aspect adds much needed variety to playthroughs, they won't feel as samey as they did in the 1.x iteration.

It also adds several mechanics to speed up elements of the game which are by default dreadfully slow, like the elevator and filing reports. And also... adds more loud jump scares to keep you on your toes.

The upgrades are well worth it as they remove the necessity for you to constantly get up from your chair to see if there are killers in your room, you get an audible warning instead. Essentially the early game becomes a little harder as you have more choices and gambles to make, but the late game can be made substantially easier / less error-prone if you play your cards right.

One flaw that made me not recommend the version 1.x iteration of this game remains; you need to play with headphones, or at least a very good sound system which you'll have to put at a high enough volume such that your neighbors are going to call the police every time the game jump scares you. One of the killers, when visiting your room, has a sound cue - a whistle. But it's really soft, so if Unreal Engine 5 is making your fans blow, and it is likely to do so especially when playing on a laptop, you're likely not going to hear it and thus you'll die. But the rest of the game is now so much better and deeper that I no longer consider it a deal breaker. 

This is a really good game... if you have nerves of steel, the patience of a saint and the focus of a painter. And noise cancelling headphones.

[b] Dead Signal [/b] may be Reflect Studio's best title yet. As a fan of their previous work (Welcome to the Game 2, Scrutinized, Masks of Deception, etc.), I was excited to dive into their latest creation, and it didn't disappoint. 

[b] Dead Signal [/b] strikes a perfect balance between accessibility and psychological intensity. It's easier to pick up than its predecessors, making it more inviting to newcomers. Yet, it still manages to deliver the same heart-pounding, nerve-wracking thrills that Reflect Studios is known for. You will fail (a lot), but the gameplay loop is satisfying enough to encourage you to try again, think more critically, and discover new strategies. 

Like their previous titles, Reflect Studios has been keen to release patches shortly after launch to fix bugs, address balance issues, and improve QOL. The game is even more enjoyable now than at launch, and I applaud the developer's attention to feedback. 

Reflect Studios has managed to capture lightning in a bottle with [b] Dead Signal. [/b] It's a must-play for fans of psychological horror and a perfect entry point for those new to the genre. The game's atmosphere and gameplay makes it worthwhile to return again and again after each failed attempt. It's a tough game, but it's tough in the best possible way. I give [b] Dead Signal [/b] five deliveries to 2C... out of five.

Dead Signal, developed and published by Reflect Studios, is a tense and methodical horror experience that combines surveillance simulation, psychological unease, and moments of real-time danger into a single claustrophobic package. Set within a decaying apartment complex under the control of a shadowy organization called ViVEX, players take on the role of an operative responsible for monitoring a network of security cameras, identifying strange occurrences, and carrying out risky field assignments. What begins as a seemingly mundane job quickly devolves into a constant balancing act between observation and survival, as the player must not only fulfill their work quotas but also avoid becoming the next casualty of the building’s unseen horrors. The premise itself is deceptively simple, but the execution turns it into a deeply unsettling exercise in paranoia and multitasking under pressure.

The core gameplay of Dead Signal revolves around the duality of control and vulnerability. Inside the surveillance room, players sit before an array of camera feeds that cover different areas of the complex. Each shift requires you to identify specific visual anomalies or suspicious activities, report them correctly, and maintain a consistent workflow to meet ViVEX’s demands. Cameras may flicker, distort, or fail altogether, forcing you to perform maintenance tasks such as rebooting systems or reconnecting feeds. Between these duties, you are sometimes required to leave the safety of your monitoring station to perform deliveries or make manual adjustments elsewhere in the building. These moments transform the game from an abstract observation puzzle into a tangible survival experience, as the player must navigate dimly lit hallways filled with potential threats, all while being aware that the very act of leaving the room exposes them to danger. This constant alternation between watching and acting creates a cycle of tension that rarely lets up.

Reflect Studios, known for its work on games like Welcome to the Game and Rides With Strangers, once again demonstrates a strong grasp of atmosphere and psychological tension. The visual design of Dead Signal is intentionally oppressive, with narrow corridors, flickering lights, and static-laden camera footage that feel authentically gritty. The apartment complex exudes a sense of decay, every corner suggesting a story of neglect and hidden suffering. The camera feeds, distorted and grainy, blur the line between digital observation and supernatural interference, making it increasingly difficult to tell what is real and what is imagined. The sound design amplifies this tension with mechanical hums, distant footsteps, and ambient creaks that hint at movement beyond your control. Every flicker of light or sudden sound becomes a potential warning sign, and the player’s mind fills the gaps that the limited visuals leave open.

While the structure of the game is engaging, it can also be demanding. Dead Signal expects attentiveness and precision, as missing even minor details in the camera feeds can lead to penalties or worse. The design encourages players to think and act like an analyst under pressure, constantly scanning for inconsistencies. However, this meticulous approach is occasionally undermined by moments of unpredictability. Certain scripted or random events—such as sudden deaths during elevator rides or unavoidable ambushes—can feel unfair or abrupt, breaking immersion rather than enhancing tension. These moments divide players between those who appreciate the unpredictability as part of the horror and those who find it unnecessarily punishing. Nevertheless, even with its spikes in difficulty and randomness, the game remains gripping, primarily because of its ability to sustain a sense of creeping dread throughout each shift.

Dead Signal’s pacing also benefits from its procedural structure. Each shift feels slightly different depending on what the player encounters, and the need to maintain focus while managing multiple tasks keeps repetition from becoming stale too quickly. Still, the game’s emphasis on monitoring and reporting may not appeal to everyone; those expecting a narrative-driven or exploration-heavy experience might find it too mechanical. The story, while intriguing, is delivered mostly through environmental details and subtle hints rather than direct exposition. Players willing to piece together clues will find themes of surveillance, control, and dehumanization woven throughout the experience, reinforcing Reflect Studios’ recurring fascination with the invasive nature of observation and the fragility of privacy.

Ultimately, Dead Signal succeeds because it captures the anxiety of being trapped in a system where you are both the observer and the observed. Its combination of methodical gameplay and unnerving atmosphere creates a distinctive rhythm that keeps players tense from start to finish. The satisfaction of correctly identifying threats or surviving a risky delivery mission is balanced by the constant fear that one mistake could bring everything crashing down. It’s a game that demands patience, attention, and a tolerance for discomfort. Though its rough edges and unpredictable moments may frustrate some, they also contribute to its identity as a raw and immersive horror experience. For players who enjoy the creeping dread of Reflect Studios’ previous works or games that make observation itself a form of terror, Dead Signal stands as an engrossing and memorable descent into digital paranoia.

Rating: 8/10

I think this is the most interesting and the most well designed Adam's game so far, but even as a fan of these games I have a limit and there's one thing that I just cannot forgive - the dumb elevator boost mechanic.

You can beat first two difficulties just fine without ever interacting with the mechanic, but if you want to beat the Nightmare mode which is the highest new difficulty with new content, you are forced to use it cause there's not enough time to not use it.

The mechanic in question is really simple - there's an elevator that you will use a lot in this game but it is quite slow. You can use a lever to make it go twice as fast in exchange for a fact that each time you use it, you roll 1d100 and if you roll 1 you die. Just like that. And keep in mind this game is already very unforgiving, you will have runs that last up to 2 hours of constant pressure and full focus because even 30 seconds can cost you the whole run.

Listen, I understand - these games were always harsh. Higher difficulties were mandatory to have an outside timer in games like WTTG2 too. Maybe not the best game design, but hey - it made a horror game more of a reflex game and I like it, in the same way I like max modes in FNAF. The problem is that this 1% mechanic doesn't involve any skill at all. You just need to do this artificial gamble if you want to beat this mode. It is just stupid. It sounds like this silly idea you and the boys have on the Discord when you think about adding mechanics to the game you play, but you would never actually add a thing like this or at the very least the QA would tell you it is not fun and you would scrap it altogether.

Personally, I think this mechanic should be scrapped altogether and just make the elevator 2x speed default on nightmare mode, this way you don't have to compensate for the additional and faster threats already in the game, or make it more interesting - put it as an upgrade in the shop, maybe even make two versions where there's a 10% gamble but upgrade is very cheap or make it safe but it is more expensive. 

Or maybe keep it as is, raise the 1% but have some kind of indicator that the next ride is deadly - that way you reward knowledge of the player. Adam already has proven plenty of times that he likes to reward players for recognizing visual and audio cues and ignoring red herrings, why not add some quiet screeching sound in the elevator or some light disturbance letting you know that you should disable the upgrade for the next 30 in game minutes if you want to be safe, after which it comes back to normal. This sounds very WTTG to me I'm surprised it isn't this way already.

I gotta give this game a thumbs down. Adam, the founder and basically sole member of Reflect Studios has been called a sociopath before, both because of his previous controversies and conduct, and because of the intense and groundbreaking subject matter of Welcome to the Game 1 and 2. To be honest, I don't think these things make him a sociopath. What makes him a sociopath is his completely deranged game design philosophy. Believe it or not, this game is actually basically the fairest one he's ever made. it seems like all of Adam's games are defined by permadeath, long playtimes that permit very few errors (the normal mode in this game takes 105 minutes to beat, other games take much longer such as Scrutinized and WTTG2) and hugely RNG-based conditions, and often unclear factors that require clarification via game guides to understand. I have nearly 14 hours on this game but, between installing and uninstalling a few times and playing on casual mode, I'd say it only took me about 7-8 hours to beat normal mode. I got very lucky on my last run and clutched up like crazy, not having made it past 1 in normal mode before that point (normal mode is 9 pm to 5 am). Based on the guides I read and my experience in reporting objects, basically every facet of the game is affected by RNG, from item spawns on the computer to Lucas, Noir, Defalco, even your signal booster. To juggle everything is hard enough, let alone when there's no guarantee of how it will behave. Some people may say this is what makes the game fun but I disagree. I feel like my skill peaked 2 hours in and the rest of the time was just spent praying that enough objects would spawn for me to be able to meet the quota. I'd say the game is 25% skill and 75% luck. If these games were much shorter I wwould have no problem with there being a reliance on luck but as I said it takes 105 minutes from start to end to win. It must be a simple matter of preference because these games are successful. My last issue with how these games work in general is that you need a guide to succeed. This game was actually pretty straightforward compared to the others, but this leads into my last major gripe with this game specifically, which is that I had to use a guide to reveal all event locations on the camera because of how infrequently events spawn. This game's major problem is that you've seen it all within a few runs, and after that is staring at the same cameras waiting for a minor change. I would have preferred higher quotas and more frequent item spawns. All in all now that I've experienced this game design firsthand I think I'll watch someone play WTTG3 on YouTube.
